Microcomputers and minicomputers differ fundamentally in their processing architecture, scale, and multi-user handling capabilities:

| Feature | Microcomputer | Minicomputer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Architecture** | Built around a single microprocessor (CPU on a single IC chip) with lower word size (8-bit to 64-bit). | Built around multiple processors or a more powerful multi-chip CPU architecture with larger word size. |
| **Processing Power & Memory** | Lower computational speed, smaller RAM capacity, and designed for single tasks. | Higher processing speed, larger RAM capacity, and support for heavy computational workloads. |
| **User Handling** | Primarily designed as single-user systems (PCs, workstations) meant for personal or standalone office use. | Designed as multi-user systems capable of supporting dozens to hundreds of concurrent users via terminals. |
proTip: Focus on the number of CPUs (single IC vs multi-chip) and concurrent users to score full marks in architectural comparison questions.
